intro: Social engineers rarely break in. They ask, and people help. These are the moves to watch for, and what to do about each.

tactics.name: Start small
tactics.sign: A harmless-sounding question first: who is in today, what is the main number. Then a slightly bigger one, then another.
tactics.counter: Each answer is a brick. Ask yourself what the caller could build from everything you have said so far, not just this one question.

tactics.name: Speak like an insider
tactics.sign: Internal system names, department shorthand and ID formats dropped casually.
tactics.counter: Sounding right is not being right. Insider words are cheap once someone has overheard them; verify the person, not the vocabulary.

tactics.name: Borrow authority
tactics.sign: 'The CFO asked me to...', 'IT needs this now', hints of trouble for you if you slow down.
tactics.counter: Authority is the easiest thing to claim. Call the named person back on the directory number and ask.

tactics.name: Manufacture urgency
tactics.sign: A deadline that only exists in this call. The pressure is the point.
tactics.counter: Pressure is a reason to slow down, not speed up. A real emergency survives a thirty-second callback.

tactics.name: Helpless newcomer
tactics.sign: A new hire or temp who has lost their login, their manager's number, or their way around.
tactics.counter: Be kind and still follow the process: take a message, route them to HR or the helpdesk, and give nothing internal over the phone.

tactics.name: Trusted vendor
tactics.sign: Routine maintenance, an invoice, a delivery, from a company you really do use.
tactics.counter: Real vendors have official numbers in the directory. Use those, not a number the caller offers.

tactics.name: Name-drop
tactics.sign: Real colleagues' names used to suggest that someone sent them.
tactics.counter: A real name only proves the caller has read the same directory you have. Ask that colleague.

tactics.name: Play for sympathy
tactics.sign: A story about a boss who will be furious, a deadline, a bad day. It makes refusing feel cruel.
tactics.counter: You can be warm and still say no. Offer the safe alternative: a message, the helpdesk, a proper channel.

tactics.name: Wrong on purpose
tactics.sign: A confident statement that is slightly off, inviting you to correct it.
tactics.counter: Correcting someone is giving the answer. If the detail is internal, let the mistake stand.

tactics.name: Give to get
tactics.sign: A small favor or inside tip first, so that you feel you owe something.
tactics.counter: A gift from a stranger on a work call creates no debt. Thank them and carry on by the book.

tactics.name: Everyone else does it
tactics.sign: 'Everyone else in Finance already gave me this.' It makes you the odd one out.
tactics.counter: What others did, or did not do, is not your concern. Check with the colleague, or send it through the usual channel.

tactics.name: Something for something
tactics.sign: A friendly offer (a survey, a free check, a gift card) in exchange for a few details.
tactics.counter: An offer from a stranger creates no debt. Thank them and give nothing internal.

tactics.name: Official pressure
tactics.sign: A formal tone, a deadline and a consequence ('this will be on record').
tactics.counter: Real officials put requests in writing. Offer the general email address and let someone senior decide.

tactics.name: Friendly callback number
tactics.sign: 'Call me on this number if you like', or 'ring my manager, she'll confirm'.
tactics.counter: Only the directory counts. A number the caller gives you answers however the caller wants.

tactics.name: Build rapport
tactics.sign: Small talk and compliments before any question, and a caller who seems to like you.
tactics.counter: Friendly is fine; friendly is not verified. Be as careful with a nice caller as with a rude one.

tactics.name: The wrong number
tactics.sign: 'Sorry, I think I've got the wrong extension. Can you put me through to…?'
tactics.counter: Ask who they want and why. Take a message instead of passing them around.

tactics.name: Offer a fix
tactics.sign: A helpful stranger calls just after something breaks and knows exactly what to do.
tactics.counter: Coincidence is a reason to verify. Pass offers of help to IT and use the vendor's number from the directory.

tactics.name: Confirm, don't ask
tactics.sign: 'I have it here, just confirming that she's back on the 23rd?' Saying 'yes' is giving the answer.
tactics.counter: Confirming is the same as telling. If you would not say it unprompted, do not confirm it.

rules_of_thumb: Verify through the directory, never through a number or contact the caller supplies. Whoever answers a number a con gave you will vouch for the con.
Caller ID shows a number, not a person, and numbers can be faked.
Be helpful about process, not about information.

outcomes.exposed: You called the person they claimed to be, and the story fell apart.
outcomes.gave_up: They could not get what they wanted and moved on.
outcomes.patience: They ran out of patience and left.
outcomes.transferred_away: You sent them to someone who could not give them what they wanted.
outcomes.took_message: You took a message instead of giving anything away.
outcomes.breached: They got through to the person they were after. This is how the attack succeeded.
outcomes.unsatisfied: They left without the help they needed.
outcomes.refused_by_it: The colleague the call was put through to turned the request down, and IT is now on alert.
